one_liner: Hand-written AVX2/AVX-512/AMX square GEMM kernels; 3-4% faster than OpenBLAS/MKL only on Granite Rapids AMX (bf16).
what_it_does: A small pthreads GEMM written with x86 intrinsics: one template entry point, simd_gemm(A, B, C, n), computes C += A*B for square n x n row-major matrices, FP32 on the AVX2 and AVX-512 paths and bf16 inputs with FP32 output on the AMX path. The ISA, thread count (NUM_THREADS) and block sizes are fixed at compile time from -march=$(TARGET); there is no runtime dispatch, no alpha/beta, no transposes and no rectangular shapes. It is a study project (README: '75-105% performance of OpenBLAS'), not a BLAS replacement.
how_it_is_fast: Goto/BLIS-style cache blocking with two levels ('superblocks' of blocks): panels of A and B are packed into contiguous, 64-byte-aligned stack buffers sized for L1/L2, then a register-blocked micro-kernel runs. The AVX2/AVX-512 micro-kernels compute a 2-row x 8-column patch of C as dot products along K (two passes of 4 columns, 16 vector accumulators) with FMAs over a pre-transposed B and finish with unpack/permute horizontal reductions; the AMX kernel keeps four 16x16 FP32 accumulator tiles and issues TDPBF16PS on two A tiles and two B tiles, with B re-laid into the VNNI pair-interleaved format by AVX-512 expand-loads inside the packing step (commit history credits that move for a 1.15-1.2x gain). Threads split the i and j dimensions of C.
when_to_use: Intel Sapphire/Granite Rapids-class CPUs with AMX, bf16 inputs and FP32 output, square n that is a multiple of the superblock size (n=4096 measured), 1-4 threads.
Learning or teaching how an AMX bf16 GEMM is built (tile config, VNNI relayout of B, packing) from about 950 lines of readable intrinsics.
Small fixed-shape experiments where you control NUM_THREADS and -march at build time and can verify results against a BLAS.
when_not_to_use: AVX2 or AVX-512 machines: it is slower than the better of OpenBLAS/MKL, 0.76x on a Kaby Lake i5-8350U and 0.82-0.87x on a Tiger Lake i5-1135G7.

Any shape other than square n divisible by the superblock size (AMX: 2048 rows, 1024 columns and depth; AVX2: 512; AVX-512: 1024 rows, 512 columns, 256 depth): there is no edge handling, and the source says matrices must be padded.

More than about 8 threads, or a thread count that does not split n into whole superblocks: the partitioning arithmetic then hands some threads rows past the end of the matrix (12 threads on the AVX2 path at n=4096 starts threads 8-11 at row 4096 and beyond), or splits K across threads that read-modify-write the same C tiles without synchronization (16 threads on AMX at n=4096). The default NUM_THREADS is nproc.
Production or redistribution: no LICENSE file, no tests beyond the bench's exact-equality check on integer matrices from utils/random_gen.py (values 0-100), no issues or releases, single author.

integration.dependencies: pthreads; OpenBLAS (built with BUILD_BFLOAT16=1 for AMX) or Intel MKL only for the bench program
integration.min_toolchain: C++ compiler with x86 intrinsics; clang 16+ or gcc 13+ for the AMX path (__bf16); the Makefile uses clang++ with -march=$(TARGET) -O3 -flto
integration.platforms: x86-64 only: AVX2 minimum, AVX-512 or AMX-TILE/AMX-BF16 paths selected at compile time; Linux assumed (pthreads, aligned_alloc)
integration.thread_safety: Spawns and joins its own NUM_THREADS pthreads per call; concurrent calls on different outputs look independent (packing buffers are per-thread stack arrays), but this is not documented

gotchas: The kernels are non-inline function definitions in gemm.h, so include it in exactly one translation unit, compiled with the right -march and -DNUM_THREADS; the installed libgemm.a holds only gemm.cxx's unused amx_relayout helper.

simd_gemm accumulates into C (C += A*B), so zero C first; the AVX paths expect B already transposed (bench.cxx calls cpu_transpose before the timed loop, so that cost is not in the AVX numbers), while the AMX path takes B as-is.

Nothing in the repository calls arch_prctl(ARCH_REQ_XCOMP_PERM); Linux traps the first AMX tile instruction until the process requests that permission (kernel xstate documentation). bench.cxx calls the BLAS first, so a standalone program must request it itself.
Per-thread packing buffers live on the stack: about 6 MiB per thread on the AMX path (4 MiB A panel plus 2 MiB B panel) and 2 MiB on AVX2, so small thread stacks will overflow.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: It is the only catalogued CPU entry with an Intel AMX bf16 kernel, so pick it to study or prototype on Sapphire/Granite Rapids. For FP32 on AVX2/AVX-512 it loses to its baseline, so GEMM_AVX2_FMA3 (2-3% over MKL 2019), cpu_gemm_opt or sgemm.c (salykova, whose article inspired this code) are better references; for production, use OpenBLAS, MKL or BLIS.
verified_claims_summary: With clang++ -O3 -flto -march=<target> at n=4096, averaged over repeated runs, the README reports 1279 vs 1229 GFLOPS (1.04x) single-threaded and 4810 vs 4675 GFLOPS (1.03x) with 4 threads for the AMX bf16 kernel on a Xeon 6972P, against whichever of OpenBLAS sbgemm and MKL bf16 GEMM was faster. On AVX2 and AVX-512 it is 13-24% slower. The README does not say which library won each row, its version or thread setting (bench.cxx does not limit BLAS threads), or which -march target was used.
status_note: Single-author hobby/study project, last commit 2025-10-08 (47 commits, 1 star, no issues); there is no license, so it is reference-only and cannot be vendored.
